name: The Mali Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Mali Empire: From Mansa to Enslaved
period: c. 1235–1460 (from Sundiata Keita to the loss of the northern provinces)

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You own every gold nugget in your empire, hear your subjects’ cases in solemn audience and receive the tribute of kings, but brothers, uncles and generals watch for a chance to take your throne.
tiers.kid: Mansa Musa of Mali gave away so much gold on his way to Mecca that gold lost value in Cairo.
tiers.rise: The throne passed within Sundiata’s lineage, to a son, brother or uncle of the last mansa, as struggles among the royal kin and the great men of the court decided; Sakura alone broke the line, and after his death the Keita returned.
tiers.why: The mansa was the supreme ruler, heir to Sundiata Keita, who defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru Kanté at the Battle of Kirina around 1235 and was proclaimed mansa over twelve allied Manding kingdoms.

tiers.name: Noble clans and governors
tiers.you: You belong to one of the quiver-bearing clans, ride to war in mail with sword and lance, and may govern a province for the mansa, collecting its taxes and keeping its garrison.
tiers.kid: Mali’s nobles fought on horseback, led the army and governed provinces for the mansa.
tiers.rise: Rank came by birth into a noble lineage, but the mansa could raise a commander to a governorship or replace a farin quickly, and a successful general, like Sakura, could reach the throne itself.
tiers.why: Below the mansa stood the great lineages of the Manding heartland.

tiers.name: Muslim scholars and judges
tiers.you: You teach the Quran and Islamic law in a trading town and judge disputes among Muslims as a qadi, and the mansa may send you to study in Fez.
tiers.kid: In Mali’s trading cities, such as Timbuktu, Muslim scholars taught students the Quran and Islamic law.
tiers.rise: Learning ran in clerical families, but the mansas sponsored scholarship, sending students to Fez and welcoming foreign scholars at court and in Timbuktu.
tiers.why: Islam had reached the Manding by the 10th century, and the mansas, their courts and the trading towns professed it, while most villagers kept the older religion.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You send your slaves with gold dust and kola nuts to Walata, trade them for desert salt and pay the mansa’s tax on every load.
tiers.kid: Mali’s merchants traded gold for salt, which camels carried in great slabs across the Sahara Desert.
tiers.rise: Trade ran in Muslim merchant families who settled along the routes; wealth bought slaves and horses, but rank still came from birth into a lineage.

tiers.name: Free farmers, fishers and herders
tiers.you: You farm millet and cotton with your kin in a village run by its family heads, send your sons with their own bows when your clan’s quota is called, and pay tribute to the mansa’s governor.
tiers.kid: Most people in Mali were farmers who grew millet and cotton and lived in villages with their relatives.
tiers.rise: Free status came by birth into a horon lineage; capture in war or in a raid could turn free people into slaves.
tiers.why: Most of Mali’s people were free farmers, members of horon lineages living in villages of related households.

tiers.name: Griots, smiths and other craft groups
tiers.you: You were born into a family of griots and sing the genealogies of the noble family you serve, whose name your words can raise or shame.
tiers.kid: Griots were musicians and storytellers who remembered the history of Mali’s kings and sang it aloud.
tiers.rise: Membership came by birth and marriage stayed within the group; a griot rose by the favour of a great patron, and the mansa’s griot was among the most influential men at court.
tiers.why: Beside the freeborn stood the nyamakala, hereditary groups who practised special crafts and married only among themselves: the griots (jeli), musicians, praise-singers and keepers of genealogies; the smiths (numu), who…

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were captured in a raid and now work your owner’s fields or carry his goods to market; sent to the army instead, you would serve the mansa as a soldier in a garrison.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people in Mali were owned by others and made to work without pay, and some were sold across the Sahara.
tiers.rise: Freedom could come by an owner’s grant, and slaves of the court and the army could win wealth and power, as Sakura, perhaps a freed slave of the royal family, did; later Mande custom set people born into a household apart from those bought or captured.
tiers.why: The enslaved, jon in Mande, were captives taken in war and in raids on neighbouring peoples, the children of enslaved mothers, and people bought in the markets.
